newsitem.title: FRANCE: BELGIAN RENAULT WORKERS HURT IN POLICE CLASH.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN RENAULT WORKERS HURT IN POLICE CLASH.

text.p: Several Renault workers were injured on Thursday when strikers from the car company's doomed Belgian plant clashed with police in the northern French city of Lille.
Police said four workers were injured while union leaders said some 20 were hurt after shoving broke out when police tried to stop demonstrators from forcing their way into the town hall.

It was the third time demonstrations against plans to close the plant have turned rough. Workers clashed with Belgian police during a march in Brussels earlier this month and with French police last month outside a car depot in the town of Wavrin.

Police said 300 workers from the Vilvoorde plant came to Lille to appeal to Mayor Pierre Mauroy, a former Socialist prime minister. After hearing that Mauroy was in Paris, they threw eggs, broke windows and tried to force their way into city hall.
Police said four workers were taken to hospital, and three of them were released quickly with slight injuries.
But the Socialist-led CFDT union said many more were hurt when police "charged" the workers. "There were some 20 injured, a few of them seriously," CFDT spokesman Daniel Richter said.
A few workers were questioned by police before the group headed back to Belgium in the afternoon.
Renault sparked an outcry when it announced on February 27 that it would close the Vilvoorde plant, which employs 3,100 people, in July to streamline its operations and cut costs.
Vilvoorde workers, who went on strike for six weeks after the announcement, had returned to work on April 14 but staged a 24-hour strike on Thursday.
Lille town officials and union leaders said they regretted the clash, which occurred after a string of misunderstandings.

The worker delegation showed up unexpectedly at the mayor's office when they had been set to meet regional Socialist leaders. Mauroy's chief of staff agreed to allow them to read a statement, but police intervened while it was being read.
"I wish they had let them finish reading the statement," chief of staff Bernard Massez said. "I had given them the go-ahead to read the statement at that point."
The workers' spokesman Karel Gacoms said events took an ugly turn. "We came to deliver a letter to the partisans of (French Socialist leader Lionel) Jospin and Mauroy. That's all," he said.
"I was really disappointed with the reception by the Socialists. It's too easy to stab workers in the back."
Courts in France and in Belgium have ruled that Renault breached the law in failing to consult staff ahead of the announcement but the rulings do not bear on the decision itself.

Renault Chairman Louis Schweitzer, former chief of staff to Socialist Prime Minister Laurent Fabius, said he was flexible on the date and could delay the closure by a few weeks or months. But he said the decision to shut down Vilvoorde was irrevocable.

Renault's French unions said in a statement on Thursday that representatives from the company's European operations were meeting for two days to discuss labour actions to protest against not only the Vilvoorde closure, but job cuts planned in France and a reorganisation of the dealer network.

Renault plans to step up job cuts in France, shedding 2,764 this year, up from 1,641 in 1996. The company last month reported a 5.25 billion franc ($906.7 million) loss for 1996, including 3.9 billion francs of restructuring charges.
Its stock fell 2.89 percent to 131.10 francs on the Paris bourse, which ended the day slightly higher. REUTER
